en: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, the Ten Prostrations to the Formless One;
to the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva in the Cool Mountain, who sits upright and gazes intently at the mind, yet even the mind cannot be apprehended.
With a sincere heart, I take refuge in and pay respectful homage to the Buddha of the Dharmakāya of True Suchness. No...
Form has no shape or image;
it has no roots and no place of abiding,
because it is neither born nor extinguished.
Homage to the one of infinite contemplations,
who neither comes nor goes,
and neither grasps nor abandons.
Because it is far removed from the six sense bases,
it transcends the three realms and is equal to empty space.
Because he is unstained by any sensual desires,
amidst all modes of conduct—
whether going or coming, sleeping or waking— he remains [unaffected].
Because they constantly abide in samādhi,
their coming and going are entirely equal;
having already dwelt in equality, they are thus established.
Because they do not disrupt equanimity,
they enter the various signless concentrations and perceive all phenomena as tranquil and pure.
Because they are free from all quiescent purity,
the Buddhas have the characteristic of space;
yet even space is without characteristic.
Because it is free from all causes and effects,
space has neither center nor periphery;
the bodies of the Buddhas are likewise so.
Because the mind is identical to empty space,
the Buddha is always present in the world,
yet remains unstained by worldly phenomena.
Because one does not discriminate the world,
all phenomena are like illusions;
as illusions, they cannot be apprehended.
Because they are free from all illusory phenomena,
one pays homage to all with equanimity;
there is neither homage nor non-homage.
With one prostration, I pay homage to all sentient beings;
together we return to the essence of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Universally, for the sake of the four debts of gratitude, those in the three realms of existence, and all beings of the *dharmadhātu*, may we be identical with suchness (*tathatā*).
I take refuge and repent; I repent with a sincere heart.
Throughout the three periods of time, I have sought the nature of sin within, without, and in between, yet in truth, it does not exist in the mind.
Since the mind is already non-existent, all phenomena are quiescent;
the three poisons and four inversions are all suchness.
Having finished the repentance, I take refuge and pay homage to the Dharmakāya Tathāgata, and with a sincere heart, I entreat you.
All phenomena are fundamentally unarisen;
since they have no arising, how could there be cessation?
This nature of non-arising and non-cessation is eternally abiding.
I only pray that all Buddhas do not enter nirvana,
but cause all sentient beings to illuminate their original nature and naturally sport within the city of nirvana.
The practitioner merely illuminates that the five aggregates are devoid of self or person, empty of both extremes;
having made this request, they take refuge and pay homage to the Dharmakāya Tathāgata.
With a sincere heart, rejoice.
The Dharma is fundamentally neither greedy nor fearful;
do not think of it as being either identical or different from the self.
Together observing the one reality, they realize non-arising;
with objectless and equal contemplation, they rejoice in all things.
Contemplating emptiness, they illuminate existence as the nature of suchness.
I only pray that sentient beings will diligently illumine their own minds.
The essence of the mind has been pure by nature from the beginning;
delusory forms and empty space are identical with the reality of wisdom.
Having rejoiced, I take refuge and pay homage to the Dharmakāya Tathāgata, and with a sincere heart, I dedicate [this merit].
Being deluded within a single room, one follows the perception of light;
because of clinging to this perception of light, the dust of the self arises.
Now, illuminating that my defilements lack intrinsic nature,
I dedicate [this merit] toward the city of non-abiding nirvana;
the five dharmas are encompassed within correct wisdom.
The eight consciousnesses are purified as the pure Mind-King;
by turning this aggregate body toward the path of Buddhahood,
one manifests constant practice throughout the four modes of conduct.
Having performed the dedication, I take refuge and pay homage to the Dharmakāya Tathāgata and make this sincere vow:
may all sentient beings ward off the six thieves,
and may the two illuminations of compassion and wisdom manifest before them.
Neither discontinuous nor eternal, free from the immeasurable;
neither empty nor existent, it is thoroughly understood as conditioned activity.
The four wisdoms and three bodies take that essence as their object.
The five eyes constantly illuminate, the three supernormal knowledges surge forth;
the three assemblies are mind-born and unimpeded;
beneath the Bodhi tree, they deliver all sentient beings.
Having made this vow, I take refuge and pay homage to the Dharmakāya Tathāgata with all reverence;
I take refuge in the Buddha’s virtues and bodhi,
so that the mind of the Way may never regress.
May I, together with all sentient beings,
enter the essence of True Suchness and take refuge in the Prajñāpāramitā of the Dharma.
Having attained the gate of the great dhāraṇī,
I vow that together with all sentient beings,
we shall enter the ocean of true suchness.
Returning to the Sangha to cease disputes,
may we together enter the ocean of harmony.
May all sentient beings likewise [attain this].
May all generate the bodhicitta;
may the three karmas be ever pure.
I pay homage to the Buddhas of the Dharma-body.
May all the assembly listen to this verse of purity for the early morning:
those who seek the bliss of nirvāṇa should train in the dharma of the śramaṇas.
Regarding the sustenance of our lives through clothing and food,
whether coarse or refined, let it be shared equally among the assembly.
This morning at dawn, all members of the assembly— senior, middle, and junior— shall purify themselves and each record the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*).
May all the assembly listen to these verses on impermanence at the hour of noon:
"If a person does not apply themselves with diligence,
they are like a tree without roots."
The leaves and flowers last until the end of the day;
though they may appear fresh for a time,
even the flowers will not remain vibrant for long.
Physical forms are also exceedingly beautiful;
yet human life is like a single moment,
difficult to repay even for a brief instant.
I now exhort all you assemblies to diligently cultivate the unsurpassed path. All you assemblies,
listen as I recite the verses on the impermanence of the evening twilight.
Once this day has passed,
life is immediately diminished accordingly.
